title: Weights & Biases
summary: The hosted experiment platform: metric dashboards, sweeps, artifacts, and model registry.
details: Weights & Biases (W&B) is the most widely used hosted ML experiment tracker: log metrics, hyperparameters, and artifacts from training with a few lines of code; compare runs on interactive dashboards; run hyperparameter sweeps; and version datasets and models. Its Tables and Reports support collaboration, and Weave adds LLM tracing. Free tier for individuals; team/enterprise plans for orgs.
integrations: PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, Hugging Face, Lightning

demo.title: Log a run to W&B
demo.program:
import wandb
wandb.init(project="lane-e-demo", config={"lr": 3e-4, "batch": 32})
for step in range(3):
    wandb.log({"loss": 1.0/(step+1), "step": step})
wandb.finish()
print("run logged")

title: MLflow
summary: The open-source lifecycle platform: tracking, projects, models, and registry — self-hosted.
details: MLflow (Databricks/LF AI) is the open standard for ML lifecycle management: Tracking logs params/metrics/artifacts to a local or remote server; Projects package code reproducibly; Models standardizes deployment flavors; Model Registry versions and stages models. Self-hostable, language-agnostic (Python/R/Java), and the default in many enterprises that need on-prem tracking.

demo.title: Log a run to MLflow
demo.program:
import mlflow
mlflow.set_experiment("lane-e-demo")
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("lr", 3e-4)
    mlflow.log_metric("loss", 0.42, step=1)
print("mlflow run complete")

title: TensorBoard
summary: TensorFlow's visualizer, now framework-agnostic: scalars, histograms, embeddings, and graphs.
details: TensorBoard started as TensorFlow's dashboard but now logs from PyTorch, JAX, and others via event files: scalar curves, histograms of weights, embedding projector, and graph visualization. It is local-first (tensorboard --logdir), free, and still the fastest way to eyeball a training run. The What-If Tool and profiler plugins extend it to fairness and performance analysis.

demo.title: Log scalars to TensorBoard
demo.program:
from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter
w = SummaryWriter("runs/demo")
for i in range(5):
    w.add_scalar("loss", 1.0/(i+1), i)
w.close()
print("run: tensorboard --logdir runs")

title: Neptune.ai
summary: Hosted tracking with strong metadata organization for teams and foundation-model scale.
details: Neptune.ai is a hosted experiment tracker emphasizing metadata structure: runs, models, and artifacts organized in queryable namespaces, with collaboration features and SSO for teams. It handles large-scale logging (foundation-model training) and offers flexible metadata schemas versus rigid run tables. Pricing is usage-based.

demo.title: Log to Neptune
demo.program:
import neptune
run = neptune.init_run(project="ws/demo", api_token="ANON")
run["params/lr"] = 3e-4
run["metrics/loss"].append(0.42)
run.stop()
print("neptune run logged")

title: Comet ML
summary: Hosted tracking with model production monitoring and LLM observability.
details: Comet ML offers experiment tracking plus model production monitoring (drift, performance) and an LLM layer (prompt tracking, evaluations). Its panels and custom visualizations suit teams that want tracking and monitoring from one vendor. Free for individuals; team plans scale by seats.

demo.title: Log to Comet
demo.program:
from comet_ml import Experiment
exp = Experiment(project_name="lane-e-demo", api_key="dummy")
exp.log_parameter("lr", 3e-4)
exp.log_metric("loss", 0.42, step=1)
exp.end()
print("comet run logged")

title: ClearML
summary: Open-source MLOps with automatic code and environment capture — 'it just logs everything'.
details: ClearML (formerly Trains) auto-captures code, packages, and configs with minimal instrumentation, plus experiment tracking, pipelines, and remote execution (agents that run jobs on queues). The open-source core is self-hosted; paid tiers add hosted scale. Its strength is low-friction adoption: wrap your script and get full provenance.

demo.title: ClearML auto-logging
demo.program:
from clearml import Task
task = Task.init(project_name="lane-e", task_name="demo")
task.connect({"lr": 3e-4})
print("ClearML captures code + env automatically")

title: Aim
summary: Open-source tracker built for 100K-run scale with a superb query UI.
details: Aim is an open-source experiment tracker designed for massive run counts: metrics stored efficiently, a Pythonic query API (run.hparams.lr > 0.001), and rich dashboards. Self-hosted, lightweight, and beloved by researchers who outgrow spreadsheets but distrust vendor lock-in.

demo.title: Log to Aim

title: DVC
summary: Git for data: version datasets and models alongside code with content-addressed storage.
details: DVC (Data Version Control) versions large files via small metafiles committed to Git, with content-addressed remotes (S3, GCS, local). dvc.yaml defines reproducible pipelines (stages with deps/outs); dvc repro reruns what changed; dvc exp run manages experiments. It is the missing piece that makes 'git clone' reproduce the data too.

demo.title: Version a dataset with DVC
demo.program:
dvc init
dvc add data/train.csv
git add data/train.csv.dvc .gitignore
git commit -m "track dataset v1"
dvc push  # to configured remote

title: Sacred + Omniboard
summary: The research classic: config-driven experiments with MongoDB-backed run records.
details: Sacred wraps experiments in config-scoped functions, capturing every parameter, and logs to observers (MongoDB, file, Slack). Omniboard visualizes the Mongo run database. Though newer tools dominate industry, Sacred remains beloved in academia for its rigor: every number traceable to a config. The pattern it pioneered — config as the experiment's identity — lives on everywhere.

demo.title: Sacred experiment

title: W&B Sweeps
summary: Hyperparameter sweeps with Bayesian search, Hyperband, and grid — orchestrated from the dashboard.
details: W&B Sweeps run hyperparameter searches with search strategies (Bayesian, Hyperband, random, grid) across agents, visualizing the search landscape live. Define the sweep in YAML, launch agents on your compute, and watch the parallel-coordinates plot. It turns tuning from ad-hoc scripts into a managed, resumable process.

demo.title: Sweep config
demo.program:
sweep = {"method": "bayes",
          "parameters": {"lr": {"min": 1e-5, "max": 1e-3},
                         "batch": {"values": [16, 32, 64]}}}
import json
print(json.dumps(sweep, indent=1)[:120], "...")

title: Optuna
summary: The define-by-run hyperparameter optimizer: pruning, TPE search, and clean Python APIs.
details: Optuna optimizes hyperparameters with define-by-run search spaces (write Python, not config files), Tree-structured Parzen Estimator sampling, and aggressive pruning of unpromising trials via median/asha pruners. Its dashboards visualize optimization history. Framework-agnostic and open-source, it is the default 'serious' tuner in research code.

demo.title: Optuna study
demo.program:
import optuna
def objective(trial):
    lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-5, 1e-3, log=True)
    return (lr - 3e-4) ** 2  # toy
study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize")
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=5)
print("best:", study.best_params)

title: Ray Tune
summary: Distributed hyperparameter tuning on Ray: scale trials across your cluster.
details: Ray Tune runs trials distributed across a Ray cluster with schedulers (ASHA, PBT, HyperBand) and search algorithms (Optuna, Ax, Bayesian). It shines when trials are expensive and many: population-based training mutates hyperparameters mid-run. For GPU-cluster tuning, it is the scalable choice.

demo.title: Ray Tune sketch

title: Hydra Configs
summary: Structured configs with composition and overrides — experiments as YAML trees.
details: Hydra (Meta) manages experiment configs as composable YAML: defaults lists, command-line overrides (lr=1e-4), multirun sweeps (--multirun), and structured dataclass configs. Combined with a tracker, the config file becomes the experiment's complete identity — rerun it and you reproduce the run.

demo.title: Hydra-style override

title: Git-Based Reproducibility
summary: Commit code, tag data, record env — the discipline that makes runs reproducible.
details: Git-based reproducibility is a discipline, not a tool: every run records the code commit hash, dataset version, dependency lockfile, and random seeds. Tools (DVC, MLflow, ClearML) automate capture, but the rule is cultural — no result counts unless its provenance triple (code, data, env) is recorded. Reproducibility checklists in papers enforce it.

demo.title: Record full provenance
demo.program:
git rev-parse HEAD > run/provenance.txt
pip freeze > run/requirements.txt
echo "seed=$RANDOM" >> run/provenance.txt
cat run/provenance.txt

title: Docker Container Tracking
summary: Freeze the whole environment in an image — runs reproduce anywhere the image runs.
details: Docker images freeze OS, drivers (CUDA), libraries, and code into a content-addressed artifact (sha256 digest). Log the image digest with each run and the environment is reproducible bit-for-bit. NVIDIA's NGC containers provide GPU-ready bases; most clusters and clouds run training in containers by default.

demo.title: Pin and record the image
demo.program:
docker build -t train:20261020 .
docker images --digests train:20261020
echo "log the sha256 digest with the run"

title: Seed Management
summary: Control every source of randomness or your 'reproduced' run will differ.
details: Seed management sets Python, NumPy, and framework RNG seeds (and CUDA deterministic flags where affordable) and logs them per run. Full determinism can cost speed (deterministic algorithms), so teams choose: log seeds always, enforce determinism for debugging, accept nondeterminism in production training with seed-averaged results.

demo.title: Seed everything
demo.program:
import random, numpy as np, torch
def seed_all(s=42):
    random.seed(s); np.random.seed(s); torch.manual_seed(s)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(s)
seed_all(42)
print("seeds set: 42")

title: Dataset Versioning
summary: Version the data like code — because the data IS the model.
details: Dataset versioning assigns immutable versions to training data (DVC hashes, Hugging Face dataset revisions, S3 versioning) and logs the version with every run. When data changes, versions change; when results shift, you diff versions. Without it, 'same code, different data' silently invalidates comparisons.

demo.title: Dataset revision pin
demo.program:
ds = {"name": "c4", "revision": "a3b2c1d", "rows": 365_000_000}
print(f"training on {ds['name']}@{ds['revision']}")

title: Model Registry
summary: Stage, version, and approve models from experiment to production.
details: A model registry (MLflow, W&B, Neptune) versions trained models, stages them (staging/production/archived), and gates promotion with approvals and tests. The registry is the handoff point between training and serving: inference loads 'production' by alias, never by path. Lineage links each version to its run, data, and code.

demo.title: Registry promotion

title: Artifact Lineage
summary: Track every artifact's parents — which data and code produced this model.
details: Artifact lineage records the DAG: dataset version -> preprocessing code -> training run -> model version -> evaluation. When a model misbehaves in production, lineage answers 'what data made this?' in one query. W&B Artifacts, MLflow, and Neptune all implement it; the discipline is logging links at creation time, not reconstructing later.

demo.title: Lineage record

title: Metric Comparison Dashboards
summary: Compare runs side by side: the daily driver of experiment iteration.
details: Comparison dashboards (W&B, Neptune, Aim, TensorBoard hparams) plot metrics across runs, group by hyperparameters, and surface the best configs. Parallel-coordinates plots reveal which hyperparameters actually matter. The practice: every tuning decision cites a dashboard view, not a gut feeling.

demo.title: Best-config query
demo.program:
runs = [{"lr": 1e-4, "loss": 0.5}, {"lr": 3e-4, "loss": 0.42},
         {"lr": 1e-3, "loss": 0.61}]
best = min(runs, key=lambda r: r["loss"])
print("best:", best)

title: Hyperparameter Search Strategies
summary: Grid, random, Bayesian, Hyperband: choose the search for your budget.
details: Search strategies trade coverage for cost: grid (exhaustive, wasteful), random (surprisingly strong baseline), Bayesian/TPE (models the landscape), Hyperband/ASHA (early-stops bad trials, best for large budgets). The modern default is ASHA + Bayesian: aggressive pruning with smart sampling. Strategy choice matters more than most people tune.

demo.title: ASHA rung schedule
demo.program:
import math
trials, eta, rungs = 27, 3, 3
keep = trials
for rung in range(rungs):
    keep = math.ceil(keep / eta)
    print(f"rung {rung}: keep top {keep}")

title: Experiment Design (A/B)
summary: Design model comparisons like clinical trials: power, randomization, and pre-registration.
details: A/B experiment design for ML: pre-register the metric and decision rule, size the sample for statistical power, randomize traffic, and correct for multiple comparisons. For offline evals, paired tests on fixed sets with confidence intervals beat 'my number is bigger'. The discipline prevents shipping noise.

demo.title: Paired comparison CI
demo.program:
import statistics
diffs = [0.02, 0.03, 0.01, 0.04, 0.02]  # model B minus A per split
m = statistics.mean(diffs)
print(f"mean diff {m:.3f} > 0 in all splits: ship B")

title: CodeCarbon
summary: Track the CO2 of your experiments — carbon as a first-class metric.
details: CodeCarbon estimates CO2e per run from hardware, runtime, and grid carbon intensity, logging it alongside loss curves. Teams set carbon budgets and report emissions in papers. Small integration cost, real accountability: the first step to greener training is measuring it.

demo.title: Track emissions
demo.program:
from codecarbon import EmissionsTracker
tracker = EmissionsTracker()
tracker.start()
# ... training ...
em = tracker.stop()
print("emissions tracked")

title: Collaborative Experiment Notes
summary: Write down what you tried and why — the lab notebook for ML teams.
details: Collaborative notes (W&B Reports, Notion-linked run docs, Markdown in repos) record hypotheses, results, and decisions per experiment. The practice that compounds: every surprising result gets a written note, and notes link to run IDs. Teams that write win; teams that rely on memory re-run dead ends.

demo.title: Note template

title: Guild AI
summary: Minimalist open-source tracking: runs as files, diffable and grep-able.
details: Guild AI takes the opposite approach from hosted platforms: runs are plain files in a local directory, diffable with standard tools, no server required. For researchers who want tracking without infrastructure, Guild's file-based runs plus its compare views hit the sweet spot.

demo.title: Track with Guild
demo.program:
guild run train.py lr=0.0003
guild compare --table
